channel.title: The Word from Nine Point Labs
channel.description: Release notes and build logs from Nine Point Labs: small, clear tools for Linux.

item.title: Sunsetting Rune, and why I'm writing in WordCraft now
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Rune is archived. WordCraft does what Rune set out to do and more, it’s open source, and it runs on Linux, so I’d rather point you there than compete with it.
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this month I started building Rune, a word processor for Linux and Omarchy with AI built right into the writing surface. Today I’m archiving it, and I’d like to tell you why.

Why I built Rune

Word processors on Linux felt like a choice between heavyweight ports and plain text editors pretending to be word processors. And every one of them treated AI as a sidebar plugin. I wanted the opposite: a fast, native app where the model is part of the page, where you can ask it to fix a paragraph and the fix lands right in your document as one undo step.

Rune got further than I expected. It went from an idea to version 0.8.7 in about two weeks, with packages for Arch, Debian and Fedora, an AppImage for most other distros, headers and footers, tables, and sign-in for ChatGPT and OpenRouter.

What I learned

Quite a lot, honestly. Rune started on LibreOfficeKit and ended up as a single Qt process that reads and writes ODF itself, because the first design had a performance ceiling I couldn’t get past. Along the way I learned to test real files instead of trusting documentation. That habit caught a bug in Qt’s own ODF writer, where a table right after a list silently disappeared when LibreOffice opened the file. By the end, Rune was checked by 504 automated tests. I’ll carry that way of working into everything I build next.

Then I found WordCraft

Recently I came across WordCraft, a fast, open-source word processor written in Rust by the ArtCraft team. I tried it, and it’s really good.

It does what Rune set out to do, and more. It has a ribbon and styles, works with .docx natively along with .odt, Markdown and more, exports PDF, and has track changes and comments, offline spelling and grammar, footnotes, a table of contents, and citations in APA, MLA, Chicago and IEEE. It runs on Linux as a Flatpak, plus macOS, Windows, FreeBSD and the web.

The part that really got me is how it treats AI. Its commands are available through a command-line tool, a JSON control channel and an MCP server, so AI assistants can work inside your documents. That’s the idea I was chasing with Rune, done in a more open way: you bring whichever assistant you like.

It’s still in development, but it’s already well past where Rune is.

Why archive instead of compete

I could keep going. But I’m one person, word processors are a lot of work to maintain, and the world doesn’t need two small open-source editors chasing the same idea when one of them is already further along. I’d rather spend my time on things only Nine Point Labs can build, and send you to the better tool.

So Rune is archived. The code stays up under the MIT license, along with the existing releases, if you’d like to learn from it or fork it. The README now points to WordCraft.

Give WordCraft a try

If you write on Linux, or anywhere really, please give WordCraft a try. The source is on GitHub if you’d like to dig in or help out.

Thank you to everyone who tried Rune or sent a kind word about it. It meant a lot.

item.title: StoryTracker takes its own screenshots now
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: StoryTracker is the World of Warcraft addon that keeps a record of your character’s adventures: quests, zones, levels, deaths, bosses, loot and more. It comes in two versions, one for WoW Forever and one for Retail. Yesterday’s releases (Forever 1.0.4 and 1.0.5, Retail 1.1.3 to 1.1.5) add automatic screenshots at the moments that make a good story, and make the addon easier to install with an addon manager.
item.content:encoded:
StoryTracker is the World of Warcraft addon that keeps a record of your character’s adventures: quests, zones, levels, deaths, bosses, loot and more. It comes in two versions, one for WoW Forever and one for Retail. Yesterday’s releases (Forever 1.0.4 and 1.0.5, Retail 1.1.3 to 1.1.5) add automatic screenshots at the moments that make a good story, and make the addon easier to install with an addon manager.

Screenshots at story moments

StoryTracker now takes a screenshot about three quarters of a second after:

  • a quest turn-in
  • a level up
  • an achievement (on Forever, only if the client fires the achievement event)
  • a boss kill
  • your first visit to a zone
  • other story moments, such as entering a dungeon or battleground, a battleground result, rare or elite kills, a new mount, epic or better loot, duels, joining a guild, a reputation standing going up, and deaths

There’s also an optional timed shot every 15 minutes, taken only when you’re out of combat, not on a loading screen and not AFK.

It takes at most one shot every 20 seconds. When two moments land together, like a turn-in that also dings, the shot is labelled with the bigger one. If you turn on “hide UI”, the interface is hidden for the shot while you’re out of combat, and it’s never touched in combat.

Each shot is logged in the addon’s saved data with its time, the file name WoW gives it, what happened, the zone and subzone, and your character’s name, realm and level. Log entries older than 30 days are dropped. Addons can’t delete files, so StoryTracker never removes screenshots itself; clean up the game’s Screenshots folder outside the game.

Turning it on and off

Screenshots are on by default, and everything is under /storytracker shots:

  • /storytracker shots on|off turns automatic screenshots on or off.
  • /storytracker shots <event> on|off controls each kind: quest, levelup, achievement, boss, newzone and story.
  • /storytracker shots timer on|off|<minutes> sets the timed shot (1 to 120 minutes, 15 by default).
  • /storytracker shots hideui on|off hides the interface for out-of-combat shots (off by default).
  • /storytracker shots log shows the last few logged shots.

Easier installs with an addon manager

Each release is now built with the BigWigs packager and comes with a small release.json file that says which game it’s for. Addon managers such as OmaForge use it to install the right StoryTracker for each client, so the Forever build goes to Forever and the Retail build goes to Retail. Installed copies also link back to their GitHub page now. Retail 1.1.5 updates the addon for the 12.1.5 client so it isn’t flagged as out of date.

Why it matters

StoryTracker’s notes are what turn a play session into a post on My Azeroth Life. Words were only half of it. Now each story moment comes with a picture taken right when it happened, and the log says exactly which shot goes with which moment, so a post can show the boss kill or the first look at a new zone instead of a stock image.

Privacy

Nothing changes here. StoryTracker has no network access, since WoW addons can’t use the internet. Screenshots are saved by WoW to its own Screenshots folder on your computer, and the log only records when and where each one was taken.

Download the latest Forever release or Retail release, or install it with OmaForge. The code is on GitHub for Forever and Retail.

item.title: Omostrich 0.3.3: tighter signing grants and safer profile pictures
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Omostrich keeps your Nostr key on your own computer and signs for your apps from the Omarchy bar. Two releases landed this morning. Version 0.3.2 finishes the profile picture hardening that 0.3.1 started, and version 0.3.3 makes your signing permissions narrower and your approval prompts clearer, especially around direct messages.
item.content:encoded:
Omostrich keeps your Nostr key on your own computer and signs for your apps from the Omarchy bar. Two releases landed this morning. Version 0.3.2 finishes the profile picture hardening that 0.3.1 started, and version 0.3.3 makes your signing permissions narrower and your approval prompts clearer, especially around direct messages.

What changed in 0.3.3

“Always allow” now covers one kind of event, not everything. Before, remembering a signing request for an app meant that app could sign any kind of Nostr event without asking again. Now the button names the kind it covers, for example “Always allow sign kind 4 (DM)”, and Authorized apps lists each app’s grants kind by kind.

Encrypt and decrypt prompts show who’s on the other end. Each request shows the other person as a shortened npub (marked “(you)” when it’s yourself) and whether you’re encrypting to them or decrypting from them. Encrypt requests also show a short preview of the plain text. A kind 4 signing request shows its recipient, and DM ciphertext is no longer previewed. None of this goes into the log.

The signer keeps running when notifications can’t. If notify-send is missing or fails, Omostrich logs it once, with an error code only, and carries on instead of crashing.

Smaller fixes:

  • Signing requests for kind 14 and kind 1059 (private messages and gift wraps) show a warning and can only be approved once, never remembered.
  • Your public key is handed out without a prompt only to an app that connected this session or that you’ve remembered. Anyone else gets asked.
  • Gift-wrap notifications look back two days, and unlocking no longer sets off a burst of old ones.

What changed in 0.3.2

0.3.1 put limits on how big your cached profile picture could be, but the file could still carry compressed metadata that expands while the image is being read. A small, hostile picture could push the panel to several gigabytes of memory. Now the daemon rewrites the downloaded picture down to just the parts needed to draw it, with no re-encoding and no new dependency:

  • PNG keeps only the image data and the colour chunks it needs. An unknown critical chunk is refused.
  • JPEG drops comments, EXIF, ICC, XMP and Photoshop data.
  • GIF keeps the first frame only.
  • WebP keeps the image data and drops everything else. Animated WebP is refused, so the placeholder shows.

Anything after the end of the image is dropped too, and a picture cached by 0.3.1 is fetched again on startup, so the cache only ever holds the stripped copy. This came out of the Omarchy plugin marketplace review (#12494).

Why it matters

Your signer should do exactly what you agreed to and nothing more. A blanket “always allow” was easy to click and hard to reason about later, and a DM prompt that doesn’t say who it’s for asks you to approve blind. Per-kind grants and clearer prompts mean you can see what each app is allowed to do and who your messages are going to.

Upgrading

Old blanket signing grants meant “sign any kind”, and there’s no way to tell which kind you had in mind, so they’re removed the first time 0.3.3 starts. The app and its other grants stay, daemon.log names each affected app, and the app asks once more for each kind it needs.

To update an existing install:

cd ~/Projects/omostrich
git pull
npm ci
./install-daemon.sh
./install-plugin.sh
systemctl --user restart omostrich

The restart matters, because the running signer keeps the old code until it’s restarted. The full notes are on the 0.3.2 and 0.3.3 release pages, the code is on GitHub, and more about Omostrich is at omostrich.com.

item.title: folderblog 0.2.10: podcast download stats with OP3
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: folderblog 0.2.10 adds one thing podcasters have been asking about: download numbers. If you publish a show with folderblog, you can now count how often your episodes are downloaded with OP3, the free, open-source podcast stats service.
item.content:encoded:
folderblog 0.2.10 adds one thing podcasters have been asking about: download numbers. If you publish a show with folderblog, you can now count how often your episodes are downloaded with OP3, the free, open-source podcast stats service.

How it works

Add one line under [podcast] in blog.toml:

analytics_prefix = "https://op3.dev/e/"

Every episode in your feeds then goes through OP3 in the form OP3 documents, including your show’s guid so OP3 can attribute downloads sooner. There’s no account to create. After a few days, your public stats page is at https://op3.dev/show/<your podcast guid>.

A few details:

  • It’s off by default. Existing feeds don’t change unless you add the line.
  • Only the feed changes. Uploads, the deploy’s size check and the player on your episode pages keep using your own address. That also means plays on your episode pages aren’t counted, only downloads from podcast apps.
  • folderblog podcast tells you whether stats are on.
  • Other prefix services work too, as long as the prefix starts with https:// and ends in /.

The My Azeroth Life podcast is already running on it.

Read this before you update

  • analytics_prefix needs 0.2.10 or newer. Older versions refuse a blog.toml that has it, so update every machine that builds the blog first.
  • If you used the old, undocumented op3 = true: it now means the same thing, and your episode addresses gain ,pg=<guid>. Podcast apps keep track of episodes by guid, so nothing gets downloaded twice.

Grab it

SystemCommand
Arch / Omarchysudo pacman -U folderblog-bin-0.2.10-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
Debian / Ubuntusudo apt install ./folderblog_0.2.10-1_amd64.deb
Fedora / RHEL / openSUSEsudo dnf install ./folderblog-0.2.10-1.x86_64.rpm
autonomix-cliautonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/folderblog

Already installed? Install the new package, then run systemctl --user restart folderblog. The packages and a plain tarball are on the v0.2.10 release, and the source is on GitHub.

item.title: omaforge 0.2.7: ready for World of Warcraft: Forever
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: omaforge is the World of Warcraft addon manager for Linux and Omarchy. Version 0.2.7 gets it ready for World of Warcraft: Forever, which launches on November 4.
item.content:encoded:
omaforge is the World of Warcraft addon manager for Linux and Omarchy. Version 0.2.7 gets it ready for World of Warcraft: Forever, which launches on November 4.

What’s new

omaforge knows the Forever release client. Battle.net installs Forever in its own _forever_ folder (product wowf). omaforge now lists that install as Forever, even before you’ve started the game for the first time and there’s no Interface/AddOns folder yet. If Battle.net hasn’t filled in a version, omaforge shows not installed yet instead of guessing. The first addon you install creates Interface/AddOns for you.

Pick it from the command line with -c forever. The beta client is still -c classic_beta.

Leftover beta folders get a proper name. If you played the beta, you may still have a _classic_beta_ folder that Battle.net no longer lists. It now shows up as Forever Beta rather than an unknown game.

Why it matters

You can have your addons in place before launch day instead of waiting for the game to create its folders. Install Forever through Battle.net, open omaforge, and set it up the same way you already do for Retail.

Get it

  • Arch / Omarchy: sudo pacman -U omaforge-0.2.7-1-any.pkg.tar.zst, then omaforge setup omarchy
  • Debian 13+ / Ubuntu 26.04+: sudo apt install ./omaforge_0.2.7-1_all.deb
  • Fedora: sudo dnf install ./omaforge-0.2.7-1.noarch.rpm
  • Any other Linux: the AppImage, chmod +x omaforge-0.2.7-x86_64.AppImage && ./omaforge-0.2.7-x86_64.AppImage. Add --install-desktop-entry to put it in your app menu.
  • With autonomix-cli: autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/omaforge

The packages are on the v0.2.7 release, and the source is on GitHub.

item.title: omaforge 0.2.8: fixes from a full QA pass
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: omaforge is the World of Warcraft addon manager for Linux and Omarchy. Version 0.2.8 is a fixes release from a full QA pass, coming the same day as 0.2.7.
item.content:encoded:
omaforge is the World of Warcraft addon manager for Linux and Omarchy. Version 0.2.8 is a fixes release from a full QA pass, coming the same day as 0.2.7.

What’s fixed

Safer uninstall. omaforge uninstall now asks before removing an addon it can’t trace to a source, such as one you wrote yourself. Without a terminal it refuses unless you pass --yes.

Damaged files no longer crash omaforge or lose data. A broken config.toml or flavors.toml gives a one-line message naming the file and the problem, and omaforge never writes over it. In the app, a red banner names the file and offers Open file, Rescan, or setting it aside (it’s kept as <name>.broken-<time>). A damaged state.json is moved to state.json.damaged-<time> and a fresh one is started, with a warning in both the CLI and the app.

Fits half a screen. The window now goes down to 640 px wide. Below 1000 px the sidebar narrows, the tabs move under the title, and less-used actions (Import/Export, and each addon’s channel, Pin, Ignore and Remove) move into a ⋯ menu. Alt+↑ and Alt+↓ switch between game versions.

Clearer messages. An unknown addon id, an AddOns folder omaforge can’t write to, an unknown root or provider, and an empty GitHub search now say what went wrong in plain words. CurseForge versions no longer show up as 1.0.1.zip or offer an update that isn’t there, check lists each addon it couldn’t check and why, and Wago says plainly that it isn’t supported yet.

Get it

  • Arch / Omarchy: sudo pacman -U omaforge-0.2.8-1-any.pkg.tar.zst, then omaforge setup omarchy
  • Debian 13+ / Ubuntu 26.04+: sudo apt install ./omaforge_0.2.8-1_all.deb
  • Fedora: sudo dnf install ./omaforge-0.2.8-1.noarch.rpm
  • Any other Linux: the AppImage, chmod +x omaforge-0.2.8-x86_64.AppImage && ./omaforge-0.2.8-x86_64.AppImage. Add --install-desktop-entry to put it in your app menu.
  • With autonomix-cli: autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/omaforge

The packages are on the v0.2.8 release, and the source is on GitHub.

item.title: Persistwise: writing that outlasts the platform
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Keep writing wherever you already do. Persistwise watches your RSS feed and keeps three copies of every new post. 30 days free, no card needed.
item.content:encoded:
I have a bad habit with blogs. I start one somewhere that feels right, write for a while, then the platform changes, the export is a mess, and the old posts sit there like a burned CD nobody can play. Geocities. LiveJournal. A host that quietly folded. Same movie, different sequel.

So I built Persistwise, and today I’d like to invite you to try it.

persistwise.com · Start a free trial

What it does

Persistwise is not another place to write. You keep blogging wherever you already do: HEY World, Substack, your own site, a newsletter, even a social feed. You give Persistwise the feed, and it does the quiet filing in the background.

It checks your feeds every 15 minutes. When it finds a new post, it keeps three copies:

  • A Wayback Machine snapshot. Persistwise asks the Internet Archive to capture the post. That snapshot lives on archive.org, it’s public, and anyone can open it without Persistwise.
  • An IPFS pin. The saved copy is pinned through Pinata onto the public IPFS network, with a content ID that points at that exact copy of your post.
  • A saved copy we keep. The post’s HTML is stored on our own storage, so there is something to fall back on when an outside service is slow or down. Only you can open it.

Your Archive page shows one line per post, with a link to each copy and a plain status for each one. If the Wayback Machine is busy, Persistwise waits and tries again later, so you don’t have to babysit anything.

RSS, Atom and JSON Feed all work. The first check takes in every post your feed lists at that moment, then new posts get picked up as they appear.

Why I wanted it

Most of us don’t lose writing because we’re careless. We lose it because the web is a rental. The landlord changes the locks, the feed dies, the pretty URL turns into a 404. The Wayback Machine is wonderful, but it only saves what someone asks it to save. I wanted a boring, stubborn librarian whose only job is to ask every time.

I also didn’t want to build another editor. I already have places I like to write, and so do you. The whole point is that you don’t have to move.

Keep: 30 days free, then $40 a year

There is one plan, called Keep. It’s 30 days free, then $40 a year, and you don’t need a card to start. Create an account, press “Start free trial,” and add your feed.

About three days before the trial ends, we’ll email you if you haven’t added a card. If you decide not to keep going, Keep pauses and nothing is deleted. Your Archive page stays readable, and your Wayback snapshots and IPFS pins stay where they are. The Wayback snapshots are kept by the Internet Archive, not by us, so they don’t depend on Persistwise at all. We don’t delete people for leaving.

A yearly price felt right for something meant to last. Longevity and a monthly habit you cancel in February don’t get along very well.

Honest notes

It’s early, and I’d rather tell you the edges up front. Each post is captured once, when Persistwise first sees it, so later edits aren’t saved. The copies are the page’s HTML only, without images or stylesheets, so they may look plainer than the original. There’s no export button yet. And Wayback and IPFS copies are public, so please only add feeds for writing you’re happy to keep public.

Give it a try

If you have a feed you care about, I’d be grateful if you’d let Persistwise keep it. Go to persistwise.com, read how it works if you’re curious, and start your free trial. If anything doesn’t work the way you expect, please write to help@ninepointlabs.com. I’d really like to hear from you.

Thanks for reading. Now go write the next one, and let the librarian do the filing.

item.title: folderblog 0.2.8: Podcast setup that works on real R2, and a Subscribe box
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: folderblog 0.2.8 is a small fix release on top of yesterday’s 0.2.7, the one that turned a blog folder into a podcast. If you tried folderblog podcast setup and it stopped at the “find it again” step, this is the release you want.
item.content:encoded:
folderblog 0.2.8 is a small fix release on top of yesterday’s 0.2.7, the one that turned a blog folder into a podcast. If you tried folderblog podcast setup and it stopped at the “find it again” step, this is the release you want.

Podcast setup works with real Cloudflare R2

After setup uploads a small test file, it checks that the file can be found again. On real Cloudflare R2 that check failed even though the upload had worked. R2 compresses some files on the way out, and when it does, its reply leaves out the file size, so folderblog read the missing size as a missing file.

folderblog now asks R2 for uncompressed replies, so the size comes back. If a reply still has no size, any successful answer counts as “the file is there”, and the size is only compared when R2 sends one. The same fix applies when a deploy checks whether an episode’s audio is already uploaded, so a working upload isn’t treated as missing. The tests now use a fake R2 that compresses the way the real one does, which is how this slipped through before.

This is the fix that got the first real show on folderblog running. My Azeroth Life was set up with it, and the story of how that show is made is here on the blog.

Easier to subscribe

  • The podcast feed has its own title. When the show and the blog share a name, the podcast feed is now called “Your Blog (Podcast)”, so feed readers and browsers can tell it apart from the blog feed.
  • A Subscribe box on the show page. The podcast page that folderblog podcast on sets up now has a Subscribe section near the top, with the full feed address ready to select and paste into a podcast app. It’s plain CSS that uses your theme’s colors, with no JavaScript.

Grab it

SystemCommand
Arch / Omarchysudo pacman -U folderblog-bin-0.2.8-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
Debian / Ubuntusudo apt install ./folderblog_0.2.8-1_amd64.deb
Fedora / RHEL / openSUSEsudo dnf install ./folderblog-0.2.8-1.x86_64.rpm
autonomix-cliautonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/folderblog

Already installed? Install the new package, then run systemctl --user restart folderblog. The packages and a plain tarball are on the v0.2.8 release, and the source is on GitHub.

item.title: folderblog 0.2.9: Fixes from a full QA pass, and podcast addresses that stay put
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: folderblog 0.2.9 is a fix release that came out of a full QA pass over this morning’s 0.2.8. That pass followed the published instructions step by step, the way a new user would, and the rough edges it found are fixed here. Most of it is podcast polish, plus a change that keeps your post addresses the same when you clone or copy a blog.
item.content:encoded:
folderblog 0.2.9 is a fix release that came out of a full QA pass over this morning’s 0.2.8. That pass followed the published instructions step by step, the way a new user would, and the rough edges it found are fixed here. Most of it is podcast polish, plus a change that keeps your post addresses the same when you clone or copy a blog.

Read this before you update

Three changes are worth knowing about first:

  • The podcast feed’s own title changes. If your show has the same name as your blog, the feed itself is now titled “Your Blog (Podcast)”, not just the link to it. Podcast apps will pick up the new name. To keep the old one, give the show its own name in podcast/index.md or with [podcast] title.
  • There’s a new file to commit: dates.toml. A post without a date of its own gets its address from the day folderblog first saw it. That date used to live only in the ignored .blog/ folder, so a fresh clone could give the post a different address. It’s now kept in dates.toml in the blog folder. After you update, the service writes it from the dates already recorded, so no address changes. If your blog is in git, commit dates.toml.
  • A new [podcast.storage] prefix setting needs 0.2.9 or newer. It pins the folder your episode files use on the audio host, so renaming the blog folder no longer changes every episode’s address. If you leave it out, nothing changes. podcast setup now writes it, and folderblog check suggests the exact line for existing shows. Older versions refuse a blog.toml that has it, so update every machine that builds the blog first.

Podcasts

  • Publishing an episode keeps your notes. folderblog podcast publish --episode (and the MCP publish_episode tool) now changes only the draft: line. Before, it rewrote the whole front matter and dropped the comments from the template.
  • check looks at draft episodes too. Problems like a missing guid show up as warnings, and the suggested guid is the same every time you run it. folderblog podcast now counts episodes left out because of a problem, and a draft no longer needs audio hosting set up.
  • No more doubled page title. The default podcast page no longer reads “Blog · Blog”.
  • S3-compatible storage is documented. With type = "s3" and no key, folderblog now tells you how to give it one (FOLDERBLOG_STORAGE_KEY_ID and FOLDERBLOG_STORAGE_SECRET, or a key file) instead of pointing you at the R2-only podcast setup.

Clearer messages everywhere else

  • Honest retry messages. A held publish only says it’ll be retried when the background service is actually running. Otherwise it tells you what to run.
  • Machines without a systemd user session. folderblog status says so plainly, and a failed install-service removes the unit file it wrote (or puts the old one back) and tells you what to do instead.
  • check names pictures nothing shows. Pictures in posts/ and pages/ that no page uses are still published, and now you’ll know which ones they are. It also notes that a robots.txt under a base_url path isn’t read by search engines.
  • Docs that don’t break. Install links are pinned to the release, building from source uses --tag, and there’s new coverage of template route headers, base_url for other hosts, machines without a systemd user session, the preview address and folderblog data examples.

Grab it

SystemCommand
Arch / Omarchysudo pacman -U folderblog-bin-0.2.9-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
Debian / Ubuntusudo apt install ./folderblog_0.2.9-1_amd64.deb
Fedora / RHEL / openSUSEsudo dnf install ./folderblog-0.2.9-1.x86_64.rpm
autonomix-cliautonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/folderblog

Already installed? Install the new package, then run systemctl --user restart folderblog, and commit the new dates.toml if your blog is in git. The packages and a plain tarball are on the v0.2.9 release, and the source is on GitHub.

item.title: folderblog 0.2.7: Your blog can be a podcast now
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: folderblog turns a folder of Markdown into a live blog the moment you save. Four releases since the last word here, 0.2.4 through 0.2.7, and the big one is 0.2.6: the same folder can now publish a podcast, with a proper feed, hosted audio, and a way for an AI agent to help without ever publishing on its own.
item.content:encoded:
folderblog turns a folder of Markdown into a live blog the moment you save. Four releases since the last word here, 0.2.4 through 0.2.7, and the big one is 0.2.6: the same folder can now publish a podcast, with a proper feed, hosted audio, and a way for an AI agent to help without ever publishing on its own.

Podcasts from a folder

Put episodes in podcast/, one folder per episode, each with its MP3 (or an MP4 if it’s a video show). folderblog builds the show page, a page for every episode, and /podcast/feed.xml. Turn it on with:

folderblog podcast on

The feed is ready for Apple Podcasts and Podcasting 2.0: every episode gets a permanent guid, and you can add transcripts, chapters, people, and optional Lightning tips. Episodes stay out of your main blog feed unless you set in_main_feed, so readers who only want posts don’t get audio in their reader.

Audio hosted on Cloudflare R2

Audio files are too big to live comfortably next to your HTML, so folderblog uploads them to Cloudflare R2 when the site deploys. The site isn’t published until the upload succeeds, which means the feed never points at a file that isn’t there yet. folderblog podcast setup walks you through it. It works with an r2.dev address or your own domain, and a custom domain is recommended. Your keys are kept outside the blog folder, so they never end up in git or on the site.

An MCP server for AI agents

folderblog mcp starts an MCP server, so an AI agent can draft, check and publish episodes for you. It only publishes after you say yes. If you’d rather do it yourself, folderblog podcast publish --episode SLUG does the same thing from the terminal. The watcher and a publish take turns, so they never build or deploy at the same time.

Templates to copy

New blogs now come with a templates/ folder holding a sample post and a sample podcast episode. Each one lists every front matter field with a short note on what it does, so you don’t have to dig through the guide to remember what draft or image does. To add the folder to a blog you already have, run folderblog templates.

Blogs keep up with updates by themselves

0.2.7 is the small one that makes the rest easier. After you install a new version, restart the service:

systemctl --user restart folderblog

The first time it starts, it adds any sample files your blogs don’t have yet, like the new templates/ folder, and refreshes the generated part of AGENTS.md. It logs what it changed. It never turns a feature on, and it never touches your design, blog.toml or your posts. A sample file you delete stays deleted.

Two fixes along the way

  • 0.2.4: draft: true in front matter now really hides a post or page from the live site, as the guide always said. Before, those were still built and listed. They now behave like files in drafts/: visible in folderblog preview and build --drafts, never in real builds.
  • 0.2.5: if you use GoatCounter, 404 pages are now counted as events named after the missing URL instead of page views, so broken links show up on their own instead of looking like visits.

Grab it

SystemCommand
Arch / Omarchysudo pacman -U folderblog-bin-0.2.7-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
Debian / Ubuntusudo apt install ./folderblog_0.2.7-1_amd64.deb
Fedora / RHEL / openSUSEsudo dnf install ./folderblog-0.2.7-1.x86_64.rpm
autonomix-cliautonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/folderblog

The packages and a plain tarball are on the v0.2.7 release. New to folderblog? See its home page, the source on GitHub, or start with the guide, or run folderblog guide.

item.title: How My Azeroth Life is made: from a WoW addon to a podcast
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: I play World of Warcraft most evenings, and for the last few weeks the game has been keeping a blog about it. Now that blog has a podcast too. My Azeroth Life tells the stories of my characters, and the My Azeroth Life podcast turns those stories into narrated episodes with music and sound effects. Both are published by folderblog, the small blog engine I make here at Nine Point Labs.
item.content:encoded:
I play World of Warcraft most evenings, and for the last few weeks the game has been keeping a blog about it. Now that blog has a podcast too. My Azeroth Life tells the stories of my characters, and the My Azeroth Life podcast turns those stories into narrated episodes with music and sound effects. Both are published by folderblog, the small blog engine I make here at Nine Point Labs.

I want to be upfront about one thing: AI does the writing and the narration. What makes it mine is that every story starts from something I actually did in the game, and I read every post and listen to every episode before it goes live. Here is how the pieces fit together.

The short version

World of Warcraft, with the StoryTracker addon
    |  log out or /reload: the addon saves its notes
    v
Companion script: one file of new events per character
    |  every morning
    v
AI writes a draft post in the Chronicler's voice  ->  drafts/
    |  I read it and move it to posts/
    v
folderblog publishes it to myazerothlife.com
    |
    v
Claude writes a script, ElevenLabs voices it, ffmpeg mixes it
    |  I listen, then say yes
    v
folderblog publishes the episode: audio on Cloudflare R2, a podcast feed

Step 1: An addon that takes notes while I play

It starts with StoryTracker, a WoW addon I wrote. It listens for game events and keeps a record of each session: quests accepted and turned in, zones and subzones, levels gained, deaths (where, and what did it), rare and better loot, reputation changes, dungeon bosses, profession skill-ups, gold earned and spent, notable kills, groups and guilds, and when I logged in and out.

WoW only lets an addon write to disk when you log out or type /reload, so the notes land in the addon’s saved file at the end of a session. There is a version for each game, and both are free on GitHub: StoryTracker for WoW Forever and StoryTracker for Retail.

Step 2: From game data to a story

A small companion script reads that saved file, compares it with what it has already seen, and writes one JSON file per character with only the new events. It also notes which game the character is in, based on which WoW folder the file came from, so Retail and Forever never get mixed up.

Every morning a scheduled job looks for those files. When it finds one, an AI agent reads the events along with a voice guide and writes a post as the Chronicler: a weathered scribe who has followed adventurers across Azeroth for decades. The guide asks for a little elevation when a moment earns it, a little grit when something goes wrong, and a dry smirk the rest of the time. One of its rules is to turn game events into world events, so a level-up reads less like a number going up and more like a character getting tougher after surviving things that should have killed them.

The draft is saved into the blog’s drafts/ folder, tagged with the game version, the character and their class. Then I read it, all of it. If it is right, I move it into posts/, and that is the whole publishing step.

Step 3: folderblog puts it online

folderblog runs quietly in the background and watches ~/Blogs, where every folder is its own blog. Moving the file into posts/ is enough. A few seconds later the post is built and live on GitHub Pages at myazerothlife.com, with no commit and no deploy command.

These are the folderblog features the blog leans on:

  • Plain Markdown files. The title comes from the first heading and the date from the filename, so a post only needs a line of tags at the top.
  • Drafts. Anything in drafts/ shows up in folderblog preview on my own machine and never on the live site.
  • Tags, with a page for each one, so you can read only Burrly’s posts or only Laotou’s.
  • A custom theme. A folderblog theme is just templates, and every blog comes with an AGENTS.md that explains them to coding agents. The parchment look on My Azeroth Life was mostly built by Claude from that file.
  • Safe builds. Every build happens in a fresh folder and only replaces the live site if everything worked, so a mistake never takes the site down.
  • folderblog check, which finds template errors, broken links and feed problems before readers do.
  • Cookie-free page counts with GoatCounter, switched on with two lines in blog.toml.

Step 4: Turning posts into episodes

Once there are enough posts, Claude Code on my workstation turns them into an audio episode. It writes a script from the posts, split into chapters, with notes for the background ambience, the sound effects, and how each line should be performed.

Each character gets their own narrator, made with ElevenLabs voice design and then kept for good. Laotou, a Pandaren monk and healer, is told by an elderly lorewalker over a pot of tea, slow and wry. Burrly, a Kul Tiran warrior, is told by an old sea captain in a Boralus tavern, faster and louder, because most of his story is him running at things. Once a character has a narrator, that voice stays theirs.

The rest of the work goes like this:

  • Narration uses the ElevenLabs eleven_v3 model, one paragraph at a time. It acts out small direction tags like [intense] or [dryly] instead of reading them aloud. Names it gets wrong are respelled only in the text sent to the voice, so “Laotou” goes in as “Lau-toe” and the script keeps the real spelling.
  • Music comes from ElevenLabs Music: a theme for each show and background beds that change with the scene, with a battle bed for the fights.
  • Sound effects and ambience come from ElevenLabs Sound Effects: a gong between Laotou’s chapters, a ship’s bell and war drum between Burrly’s, plus sword clashes, war horns and the noise of a busy tavern.
  • Mixing is done with ffmpeg. The music and ambience dip under the voice, the effects sit in the gaps, the whole thing is brought to a normal podcast loudness, and chapter markers are embedded in the MP3.
  • Checking. Every clip is run back through speech-to-text and compared with the script, so a missing line or a made-up one gets caught. Then I listen to the finished episode myself.

Every piece of music and every effect is saved to a shared library and reused, so each one is only paid for once.

Step 5: folderblog publishes the podcast

The podcast is part of the same blog folder. folderblog podcast on added a podcast/ folder, and each episode is a folder inside it with its show notes, the MP3 and a chapters file. From that, folderblog builds:

  • A show page at /podcast/ with a Subscribe box, and episode pages with a player and clickable chapters.
  • Its own feed at myazerothlife.com/podcast/feed.xml, separate from the blog’s feed, with the iTunes and Podcasting 2.0 tags podcast apps look for: a permanent show ID, chapters, people, and an optional Lightning address for tips.
  • Audio on Cloudflare R2. The MP3s never go into git or the website itself. folderblog podcast setup walked me through connecting R2 once. When an episode is published, folderblog uploads the audio first, checks that it is really online, and only then updates the site and feed, so the feed never points at a missing file.
  • Drafts. An episode starts as a draft that is never uploaded. I listen to it, and only after I say yes is it published.

folderblog also has an MCP server, so an agent can set up a draft episode, write its notes and chapters, check it, and publish it only after you say yes.

What’s next

From here on there is one show a week for each game. The Retail show comes out on Sunday nights. The Forever show comes out on Monday nights, starting after WoW Forever launches on November 4. Both go in the same feed, tagged by game, and each covers every character who had an adventure that week, with a short transition between them. If nobody played that version, there is simply no show that week.

Have a listen

  • Episode 1: The Chronicle of Laotou, 23 minutes in 5 chapters
  • Episode 2: The Chronicle of Burrly, 26 minutes in 8 chapters
  • The feed for your podcast app: https://myazerothlife.com/podcast/feed.xml

If you have a folder of writing that you’d like to turn into a blog, or a blog that you’d like to turn into a podcast, folderblog is free and runs on Linux. And if you listen to an episode, I’d love to hear what you think.

item.title: A relay on your own PC: thinking out loud about FIPS and local sync
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Last night Lez (lez@nostr.hu) left a reply that has stuck with me:
item.content:encoded:
Last night Lez (lez@nostr.hu) left a reply that has stuck with me:

Please also consider FIPS and a relay running on the PC to sync with mobile. The advantage: when PC and mobile are on the same LAN, it connects directly, saving a round-trip to the Internet and back, which is a game changer when decrypting DMs for example.

I think Lez is right, and it lines up with something I have wanted for Omostrich for a while: reaching my own machines without leaning on Tailscale or a VPN. So I spent some time looking at what already exists. This is not an announcement. It is me thinking out loud, and I would love to hear from people who have tried any of this.

Why a relay on the PC makes sense

Right now most of us send every note, reaction and DM out to a relay somewhere on the internet, and then pull it back down onto the phone sitting next to the laptop. That works, but it is slow, it depends on someone else’s server being up, and it means your data is only as private as that relay.

A relay on your own computer flips that around. Your PC holds a full copy of your own events. Your phone talks to it directly when you are home, and everything syncs out to the public relays when it needs to. Decrypting a long DM thread from a box on the same desk is a very different experience from fetching it across the internet.

FIPS

FIPS (Free Internetworking Peering System) is a mesh network where each machine’s identity is a Nostr key. Every node gets a private IPv6 address tied to its npub, finds peers by publishing signed adverts on Nostr relays, and uses encrypted Nostr messages to punch through home routers. It can run over the internet, a LAN, Tor, Bluetooth, Ethernet and even radio. Ordinary tools like ssh or a ws:// relay URL just work on top of it.

It is exactly the shape of thing I had in mind. It is also young. The README says the protocol and APIs are not yet stable, a security audit is the top item on the roadmap, and the most recent release was mostly security fixes. That is healthy for a project at this stage, and it is moving fast, but I would not lean on it for anything important yet. I do want to run it on my own machines and help where I can with testing and bug reports.

Other options I looked at for the “reach my own machine” part:

  • Tailscale or Headscale. Still the most reliable choice today. Headscale lets you run the coordination server yourself.
  • Iroh. A mature Rust library (1.x) that connects directly when it can and falls back to a relay server you can host yourself. If Omostrich ever needs its own peer-to-peer link, this is probably where I would start.
  • Yggdrasil and Reticulum. Older mesh projects. Reticulum is strong for radio and offline use. Neither uses Nostr identities.
  • Tor onion services. Very mature and work through any router, but slow. Citrine on Android already offers this.

The relay part already mostly exists

The nice surprise is that the relay and sync side does not need much new work. NIP-77 (negentropy sync) lets two relays compare what they have and only send the difference.

  • strfry can sync both ways with a relay in a single command, filtered to your own pubkey. FIPS even ships an example of running strfry reachable only over the mesh.
  • Haven is a personal relay with import and backup built in.
  • nostr-relay-tray is a desktop relay app, and as Lez points out, there is work there toward exactly this kind of syncing.
  • Citrine does the same job on Android.

relay.pleb.one already answers NIP-77 sync requests, so pulling your history down to a local relay works today. Pushing back up works for members of the relay.

What I might do with this

Nothing is decided, and I am trying hard not to start new projects this month. But the first experiment is small and needs no new code:

  1. Run strfry on my own PC with a timer that syncs my events with relay.pleb.one.
  2. Point my phone at it over the LAN, and later over FIPS.
  3. If that holds up, package it as a simple “pleb.one local” setup for Omarchy so anyone on the relay can do the same.

I would only build something new if the existing tools fall short, and I suspect they will not.

Thank you to Lez for the nudge. If you are running a local relay already, or you have been testing FIPS, I would really like to hear how it is going.

item.title: Omostrich 0.3.1: profile pictures loaded safely
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Omostrich keeps your Nostr key on your own computer and signs for your apps from the Omarchy bar. Version 0.3.1 is a small security release. It changes how the panel shows your profile picture and attachment previews, so a picture someone else controls can’t stall or overload the panel.
item.content:encoded:
Omostrich keeps your Nostr key on your own computer and signs for your apps from the Omarchy bar. Version 0.3.1 is a small security release. It changes how the panel shows your profile picture and attachment previews, so a picture someone else controls can’t stall or overload the panel.

What changed

Your profile picture is fetched with limits. Before, the panel took the picture URL from your Nostr profile and handed it straight to Qt to download and decode. Now the panel never loads that URL itself. While Omostrich is unlocked, the signer daemon downloads the picture with firm limits:

  • a 10 second timeout and a 1 MB size cap, enforced even when the server doesn’t say how big the file is
  • PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP only, checked by both the content type and the file’s own signature, so SVG or HTML dressed up as an image is turned away
  • at most 2048 by 2048 pixels, checked before anything is decoded, so a tiny, highly compressed file can’t blow up into a huge image in memory

A picture that passes is kept as a local copy in ~/.local/share/omostrich/, readable only by you, and the panel shows that copy at a small size. It isn’t fetched again on every restart. If a picture fails any check, you’ll see the placeholder instead, and the reason goes in daemon.log.

Attachment previews show your own file. When you attach an image to a note, the preview now shows the local file you just uploaded rather than loading it back from the Blossom server, and only when it’s within the same limits. The Blossom server’s reply is capped at 64 KB, and every image in the panel now has a bounded decode size.

Why it matters

Your profile picture URL is public data that anyone can point anywhere, and the panel sits right next to your key. Keeping remote downloads out of the panel, and behind tight limits in the daemon, means a slow or hostile image server can’t hang the bar or eat your memory. The issue was raised in the Omarchy plugin marketplace review (#12494), and nothing else in the panel loads remote content.

Get it

To update an existing install:

cd ~/Projects/omostrich
git pull
npm ci
./install-daemon.sh
./install-plugin.sh
systemctl --user restart omostrich

The restart matters, because the running signer keeps the old code until it’s restarted. The full notes are on the 0.3.1 release page, and more about Omostrich is at omostrich.com.

item.title: Omostrich 0.3: log in to Nostr apps by QR code
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Omostrich keeps your Nostr key on your own computer. It holds the key encrypted, unlocks from the Omarchy bar, posts notes, and signs for other Nostr apps over NIP-46 (remote signing) so those apps never see your key. Version 0.3.0 makes that last part much easier: you can now connect a phone app by scanning a QR code instead of copying long connection strings around.
item.content:encoded:
Omostrich keeps your Nostr key on your own computer. It holds the key encrypted, unlocks from the Omarchy bar, posts notes, and signs for other Nostr apps over NIP-46 (remote signing) so those apps never see your key. Version 0.3.0 makes that last part much easier: you can now connect a phone app by scanning a QR code instead of copying long connection strings around.

What’s new

Show a QR code, scan it from your phone. Under Remote signing there’s a new QR button next to Copy. It shows your bunker:// connection string as a QR code, which a phone app such as Amethyst can scan to log in with a remote signer. The string is public (your public key and your NIP-46 relays, no secret), and the app’s connect request still shows up in Omostrich for you to approve, like any other.

Connect apps that show their own QR code. Some apps go the other way and display a nostrconnect:// code. Scan QR reads it with your laptop camera, or Paste code takes a copied string. Omostrich checks the code, answers the app on the relays it names, and adds it to Authorized apps under its own name. After that it keeps listening for that app after every unlock until you revoke it.

The camera is handled carefully. Frames go straight to the decoder and are never saved, and the camera turns off as soon as a code is read, when you cancel or close the preview, or after two minutes. Laptop webcams are fixed-focus and these codes are dense, so hold the code inside the guide box about 25 to 35 cm away. Even then, reading a phone’s code with a laptop camera can be unreliable, so the bunker QR is the dependable direction.

Approve all or deny all. Right after you log in, Amethyst signs a burst of events at once. When several requests are waiting, you can now settle every one on screen in one click, each just this once. Anything that arrives after you click still waits for its own answer.

Smaller fixes

  • Always allow no longer overwrites an app’s saved relays or name.
  • A request delivered twice is handled only once.
  • daemon.log now records each request’s method (such as sign_event) and whether the reply worked, never the content of the request or the reply.
  • The About page’s privacy statement now covers camera use, the relays a scanned app names, and the new log details.

Also new since 0.2

Omostrich 0.2.1 added an optional listener on your Tailscale address so your own devices can reach the signer with a token, and NIP-46 requests are now heard on every bunker relay, not just your posting relays.

Get it

The QR features need three extra packages. Everything else works without them:

sudo pacman -S qrencode ffmpeg zbar

To update an existing install:

cd ~/Projects/omostrich
git pull
npm ci
./install-daemon.sh
./install-plugin.sh
systemctl --user restart omostrich

The restart matters, because the running signer keeps the old code until it’s restarted. More about Omostrich is at omostrich.com.

item.title: fm-cli and Autonomix CLI get their own websites
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Two of the terminal tools now have proper homes on the web: fm-cli.ninepointlabs.com and autonomix-cli.ninepointlabs.com. Until today, the only way to learn about either one was its GitHub README.
item.content:encoded:
Two of the terminal tools now have proper homes on the web: fm-cli.ninepointlabs.com and autonomix-cli.ninepointlabs.com. Until today, the only way to learn about either one was its GitHub README.

What’s on them

Each site is one page that answers the questions you’d have before installing: what the tool does, how to install it on your system, and how to get started. Both link straight to the latest release, and the full command reference stays in the README for when you need it.

fm-cli is Fastmail from the terminal: a full-screen mail app, commands that print JSON, and a live watch that follows your mailbox over Fastmail’s push connection. The site walks through all of it, including offline mode, the two-week calendar agenda and contacts, and how sign-in keeps tokens in your system keyring. It also shows every way to install it:

# On Omarchy
omarchy-mise-install github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli fm-cli

# With mise anywhere else
mise use -g github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli@latest

There are .pkg.tar.zst, .deb and .rpm packages and plain tarballs for Linux and macOS too. The README’s screenshot was also swapped for one showing sample mail.

Autonomix CLI installs and updates apps straight from GitHub Releases. The site covers the package formats it understands, how it detects what’s already installed, the JSON output for scripts, and how it fits into Omarchy: the bar widget and the post-update hook that updates your apps whenever you run omarchy update. Install steps for Debian and Ubuntu, Fedora and Arch are right there, along with the full command list.

Why it matters

A website is easier to share and easier to read than a repository. If you’ve been sending someone a GitHub link to explain what fm-cli or Autonomix CLI is, you can send them the site now. Nothing changes in the tools themselves, so there’s nothing to update.

item.title: Seven Nine Point Labs apps now run on any Linux, with AppImages
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Nine Point Labs apps are made for Omarchy first, and that isn’t changing. But they shouldn’t stop at Omarchy. As of today, seven of them also run on Ubuntu, Fedora, openSUSE and most other Linux distributions: every release now comes with an AppImage that runs on most x86_64 Linux systems and fits properly into your desktop.
item.content:encoded:
Nine Point Labs apps are made for Omarchy first, and that isn’t changing. But they shouldn’t stop at Omarchy. As of today, seven of them also run on Ubuntu, Fedora, openSUSE and most other Linux distributions: every release now comes with an AppImage that runs on most x86_64 Linux systems and fits properly into your desktop.

What’s new

These releases went out today, each with a -x86_64.AppImage attached next to the usual packages:

  • Repokase 0.2.5
  • Jubako 0.4.7
  • Dogear 0.1.1
  • omaforge 0.2.6
  • Rune 0.8.6
  • Bahá’í Reader 0.1.4
  • Hyprfall 0.1.4

The Python and Qt apps carry their own Python and Qt inside the AppImage, and Hyprfall carries its own Quickshell and Qt, so there’s nothing else to install. They run on most systems from about 2021 or 2022 on (glibc 2.34 or newer, 2.35 for Hyprfall): Ubuntu 22.04 and later, Debian 12 and later, Fedora, openSUSE and others.

It behaves like a real app

Download it, make it executable and run it:

chmod +x dogear-0.1.1-x86_64.AppImage
./dogear-0.1.1-x86_64.AppImage --install-desktop-entry

--install-desktop-entry puts the app in your application menu with its proper icon, so it shows up correctly in your launcher, taskbar and dock. Dogear also offers itself for PDFs, and Jubako opens .jubadb files. If you’d rather let a tool manage it, Gear Lever and AppImageLauncher both pick these up. Each AppImage has a .sha256 and a .zsync file next to it for checking and updating.

A few app-specific notes

  • Repokase and Dogear now follow your desktop’s light or dark setting when they’re not on Omarchy. On Omarchy they still follow your theme.
  • Dogear 0.1.1 also adds an About screen and works better in narrow windows, like half a screen in a tiling window manager.
  • Rune 0.8.6 packages for Arch, Debian and Fedora now install Rune’s AppStream info and icons in every size, so software centers and menus show it properly.
  • Bahá’í Reader 0.1.4 adds a Flatpak bundle as well, bahai-reader-0.1.4-x86_64.flatpak. It brings its own Python and GTK through the GNOME runtime, so it runs even where your system GTK is too old. It’s a download on the release page, not a Flathub listing. If your system’s Python or GTK is too old for the AppImage, the AppImage now tells you so and points you to the Flatpak.
  • Hyprfall 0.1.4 now needs Quickshell 0.3 or newer. Fedora’s Quickshell is older than that, so the Fedora package is gone and Fedora players should use the AppImage, which brings Quickshell 0.3.2 with it.

Get them

On Omarchy and Arch, nothing changes: install the .pkg.tar.zst from the release, or let Autonomix CLI pick the right download and keep the app updated:

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/dogear

On any other Linux, grab the AppImage from the release pages above. From here on, every new Nine Point Labs desktop app release ships an AppImage, and a Flatpak bundle will join it on the release page starting with each app’s next release.

item.title: Autonomix CLI 0.4.3: one password prompt for Update All
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: If you track several GitHub-release apps with Autonomix CLI and hit “Update All”, you probably met the same password dialog over and over. 0.4.3 fixes that: updating several apps now asks for your admin password once.
item.content:encoded:
If you track several GitHub-release apps with Autonomix CLI and hit “Update All”, you probably met the same password dialog over and over. 0.4.3 fixes that: updating several apps now asks for your admin password once.

What changed

Before, autonomix-cli update (and “Update All” from the Omarchy bar widget) installed each update on its own, so polkit asked for your password once per app. Now it downloads every update first, then installs them all in a single pacman -U, apt-get install or rpm -Uvh call. One install, one prompt.

Failures are clearer too:

  • A failed download only affects that app. It’s reported as failed, and the rest still install.
  • A failed install names everything in it. If the combined install fails, every app in the batch is reported with the installer’s error.
  • Cancelling says so. Closing the polkit dialog now shows “authentication cancelled” instead of a bare exit code.

The --json output is unchanged, so the bar widget keeps working as it is. No update needed on that side.

Also new since the last post

0.4.2 added an About screen. Press i in the TUI to see the version, the MIT license, a support email and a privacy statement, or run autonomix-cli about from the command line.

Get it

Autonomix CLI tracks itself, so if you already have it:

autonomix-cli update

New here? Add it once and it keeps itself current:

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/autonomix-cli

Packages for Arch, Debian/Ubuntu and Fedora (amd64 and arm64) are on the v0.4.3 release.

item.title: Dogear: a PDF reader for studying, made for Omarchy
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Class handouts, workbooks and textbooks mostly arrive as PDFs now, and most PDF readers treat them as something to look at, not something to work in. Dogear does what you’d do to a paper textbook: highlight in several colors, write notes next to what you highlighted, fold the corner of a page, and fill in the blanks on a worksheet. When you’re done, it exports everything to Markdown, for example straight into your Obsidian vault.
item.content:encoded:
Class handouts, workbooks and textbooks mostly arrive as PDFs now, and most PDF readers treat them as something to look at, not something to work in. Dogear does what you’d do to a paper textbook: highlight in several colors, write notes next to what you highlighted, fold the corner of a page, and fill in the blanks on a worksheet. When you’re done, it exports everything to Markdown, for example straight into your Obsidian vault.

dogear.ninepointlabs.com (with a narrated demo video) · v0.1.0 on GitHub

Mark it up like paper

Select text and press 1 through 5 to highlight it in yellow, green, blue, pink or purple, or press a to highlight and write a note in one go. Hover a highlight to read its note; notes also show in the sidebar and as markers in the margin. Press b to bookmark a page (it gets a folded corner, named after its table of contents entry), and keep general notes about the whole document with Ctrl+N.

Dogear remembers the page, scroll position and zoom for every file, so opening a handout again puts you back where you stopped.

Fill in the blanks

This is what sets Dogear apart. Worksheets leave lines for answers, and in Dogear you just click the line and type. There’s no text box to place: it finds the line in the rendered page (drawn rules, runs of underscores, dotted lines), writes on it in blue ink at the size of the page’s own text, and shrinks a long answer to fit a short blank. Tab jumps to the next blank, so a whole fill-in-the-blank page can be done from the keyboard. Ruled lines under a question become one answer that wraps from line to line.

A library that remembers your marks

With no PDF open, Dogear shows a library of every PDF you’ve opened, with how many highlights, notes, answers and bookmarks each has. Search reaches inside your marks too, so a word you highlighted three weeks ago finds its handout. You can sort, file documents under categories, and give them your own names (“Book 3: Children’s Classes” instead of a 60-character file name) without renaming the file.

Dogear never changes your PDFs. It keeps a copy of every PDF you mark up, so your marks always have their PDF even if the original is moved or deleted. Everything lives in one folder, ~/Documents/Dogear by default, that you can sync between computers with Syncthing, Dropbox or Google Drive. If two computers change the same document before syncing, Dogear merges the conflict copy back in and keeps every mark from both. It also notices a re-download or new edition of a book you’ve marked up and offers to bring your marks over.

Into Obsidian

Ctrl+E writes a Markdown file per PDF: document notes first, then one section per page with highlights as quotes (page and color included), each note under its highlight, bookmarks, and every worksheet answer under its full question, so the export reads without the PDF. Categories come along as Obsidian tags. Point the export folder at your vault in Settings and your study notes land where the rest of your notes live.

Native to Omarchy

Dogear is keyboard first, with Vim-style reading keys (j/k, J/K for pages, / to search) and Ctrl for commands, leaving Super to Hyprland. It follows your Omarchy theme and repaints the moment you run omarchy theme set, and it makes room in narrow tiling windows. No account, no network access and no telemetry.

Install v0.1.0

On Arch and Omarchy, install it with autonomix-cli, which also keeps it updated from GitHub Releases:

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/dogear

Or download dogear-0.1.0-1-any.pkg.tar.zst from the release page and run sudo pacman -U dogear-0.1.0-1-any.pkg.tar.zst. pacman pulls in pyside6 and qt6-webengine (for the Qt PDF library). Dogear then shows up in your app launcher and can open PDFs from the file manager.

MIT licensed. Questions or bugs go to help@ninepointlabs.com or the issue tracker.

item.title: folderblog 0.2.3: Better link previews, optional visitor counts, and safer deploys
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: folderblog turns a folder of Markdown into a live blog the moment you save. Two releases since the last word here, 0.2.2 and 0.2.3, make what it publishes look better when it’s shared and searched, add an opt-in visitor counter, and stop a blog kept in git from deploying half-finished work.
item.content:encoded:
folderblog turns a folder of Markdown into a live blog the moment you save. Two releases since the last word here, 0.2.2 and 0.2.3, make what it publishes look better when it’s shared and searched, add an opt-in visitor counter, and stop a blog kept in git from deploying half-finished work.

Share images for every post

Add image: to a post’s front matter, either a path inside the blog or a full URL, and it becomes that post’s og:image and twitter:image. folderblog writes it as an absolute URL and adds the width and height when the file lives in the blog. Posts without one fall back to static/og-default.png, or to a new optional image key in blog.toml.

---
title: "My post"
image: img/cover.jpg
---

folderblog check warns when the image doesn’t exist, so a typo doesn’t quietly ship a broken preview card.

Search engines get the whole picture

The default theme now gives every page a meta description, a canonical link, the full set of OpenGraph tags, and a twitter:card. Post pages carry BlogPosting structured data (JSON-LD), and the home page has a single h1 with the site title.

folderblog also writes a robots.txt by default that allows everything and points to the sitemap. If your blog has its own static/robots.txt, or your theme provides one, yours wins. And check now warns when blog.toml has no description.

If you keep your own copy of the theme in theme/, your templates are left alone. Copy the new default theme’s _layouts/base.html and post.html to pick up the tags, and run folderblog agents-md --write in each blog folder to refresh its AGENTS.md.

Optional visitor counts with GoatCounter

Want to know whether anyone reads the thing? Add one section to blog.toml:

[analytics]
goatcounter = "https://you.goatcounter.com"

Every rendered page gets GoatCounter’s cookie-free counting script, with any theme and no template edits. It’s off by default: with no [analytics] section the output is byte-for-byte what it was before. It’s never added by preview or build --drafts, so your own drafting doesn’t count as visits, and check flags an invalid URL.

Hold deploys while you’re mid-git

0.2.2 added deploy_branch for blog folders you keep in git:

deploy_branch = "main"

With it set, folderblog only deploys while the folder is a checkout of that branch. On another branch, a detached HEAD, or in the middle of a merge, rebase or cherry-pick, the deploy is held and shows as held: ... in folderblog status. It retries on its own once you’re back on the branch. Leave it unset and nothing changes. This blog runs with it on.

One note for both releases: older versions reject unknown keys in blog.toml, so upgrade before adding image, [analytics] or deploy_branch.

Grab it

SystemCommand
Arch / Omarchysudo pacman -U folderblog-bin-0.2.3-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
Debian / Ubuntusudo apt install ./folderblog_0.2.3-1_amd64.deb
Fedora / RHEL / openSUSEsudo dnf install ./folderblog-0.2.3-1.x86_64.rpm
autonomix-cliautonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/folderblog

The packages and a plain tarball are on the v0.2.3 release. New to folderblog? Start with the guide, or run folderblog guide.

item.title: Hyprfall: a jungle platformer native to Omarchy
item.dc:creator: Tim
item.description: Remember the summer of ’82? One stiff red button, a thousand screens of jungle, and a crocodile that still owes you an apology. Hyprfall is that spirit as a native Omarchy app: swing on ethernet cables, hop the anti-AI garden gnomes, and find 32 treasures before the clock runs out.
item.content:encoded:
Remember the summer of ’82? One stiff red button, a thousand screens of jungle, and a crocodile that still owes you an apology. Hyprfall is that spirit as a native Omarchy app: swing on ethernet cables, hop the anti-AI garden gnomes, and find 32 treasures before the clock runs out.

hyprfall.ninepointlabs.com · v0.1.0 on GitHub

What you are playing

You get twenty minutes, three lives, and 255 screens of jungle arranged in a ring. Each screen comes from one byte walked with a reversible 8-bit LFSR, so walking left brings back exactly the screens you passed. Same jungle every game; learn it like it is 1983.

Between you and the loot: tarballs, a purple pool of node_modules, rolling logs that knock points off, a python that will kill you (should have used Ruby), dumpster fires, and a pit of garden gnomes waving signs like RTFM, STOP VIBING, and NO AI. When they are quiet, their hats are stepping stones. When they yell, get off.

The signature move is the ethernet cable. Jump for the plug, ride it across, and let go with ↓ or Space. Hold the direction you want and the swing flings you that way. Fumble it and enjoy the tar. Underneath, a tunnel lets you skip three screens up top — watch for firewalls and the bug that works on its machine.

Treasure is worth chasing: Golden Keycaps, Rubies, Arch Idols, and Hypr Crystals. Find all 32 before 0:00.

Native to Omarchy, not bolted on

Hyprfall runs on Quickshell — the same engine as the Omarchy shell. No Electron, no browser, no emulator. On Omarchy there is nothing extra to install.

The whole jungle wears your theme: canopy green, swamp blue, tee logo accent, gnome hats and coats. Run omarchy theme set mid-game and it repaints while you play. Skin, hair, and wood stay fixed so the hero (long wavy hair, beard, black tee) stays recognisable on every theme.

It opens as a centered floating 16:10 window on Hyprland; launch again and it focuses the one already open. F11 goes fullscreen. Vim keys work: h/l to run, k/j to climb.

There is an original adventure-rock soundtrack and a dozen sound effects, all generated from scratch by a little synth in the repo. High scores live in ~/.local/state/hyprfall/save.json.

Grab v0.1.0

Packages for Arch/Omarchy, Debian, and Fedora ship on the v0.1.0 release. Each package was installed on its distro and the game run headless (hyprfall --selftest) before the release went out.

autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/hyprfall

Or install the .pkg.tar.zst, .deb, or .rpm from the release page, then launch Hyprfall from the app launcher or run hyprfall. Away from Omarchy you need a Wayland desktop with Quickshell; without an Omarchy theme it falls back to a built-in Tokyo Night palette.

MIT licensed. An affectionate parody — nothing from any 1982 cartridge, and the protesting gnomes are a joke at a debate, not at anyone in it. Some of them make good points, and they all have excellent signs.
